ledger.note: c. 1110: the Meitei kingdom of Kangleipak at Imphal. The court chronicle 'dates the first king to 33 CE' (Parratt and Kamei suspect astrology, and the first seven kings are said to reign to 411 CE); the Loiyamba Shinyen, Manipur's 'first written constitution', is 'dated to 1110 ad' (the page also says early 12th and late 11th century). 1110 is the earliest date that shows a state; the real founding is older and not datable from the pages opened. [Reviewer sa-06-x, 2026-10-25: the Kingdom of Manipur infobox gives the span '1110–1949'; source set to that page and confidence raised to 2 (the region is still the valley core, not named by the page).]

1709: under Gharib Niwaz (Pamheiba, 1709-1748) 'the kingdom's name changed from Kangleipak to Manipur'. The page gives the reign, not the year of the change; the Kingdom page says the present dynasty began in 1714.

ledger.note: 1819: Burma occupies Manipur. 'Burmese forces occupied Manipur during King Marjit's reign' in the Seven Years Devastation (Chahi Taret Khuntakpa), 1819-1826.

ledger.note: 1826: the Burmese are out of Manipur 'and then from Kabaw Valley by 1826' (History: the occupation 1819-1826).
1826: the Kabaw Valley. Gambhir Singh expelled the Burmese from Manipur 'and then from Kabaw Valley by 1826'; the page says nothing of how long before Burma it was Manipur's.
1834: the Kabaw Valley goes back to Burma 'after prolonged negotiation' (some Manipuri scholars call it a lease); Manipur received Rs 6,370 a year as compensation.

They are drawn from 1891, the year the page makes Manipur a princely state, as a bridge; the earlier kingdom may have held them.

ledger.note: 31 March 1891: the Anglo-Manipur War. Quinton 'ordered the arrest of senapati in his own fort', the arrest failed and the residency was besieged; British columns from Silchar, Tamu and Kohima converged on Imphal.

ledger.note: 27 April 1891: 'the Silchar, Tamu and Kohima columns united, capturing Imphal after finding it deserted'; the Kingdom page says the British briefly annexed Manipur under the doctrine of lapse.

ledger.note: 27 April 1891: the war ends with the fall of Imphal.

ledger.note: 22 September 1891: 'the British placed the young boy Meidingngu Churachand on the throne'; Manipur 'was converted into an Indian princely state subject to British Paramountcy'.

15 October 1949: the kingdom merges with India. The agreement signed on 21 September 1949 'took effect 15 October 1949'; Manipur became a Part C State under a Chief Commissioner (Union Territory 1956, full state 21 January 1972).

notes:
Written 2026-10-25 by sa-06-x. A state Cliopatria lacks: cliopatria_names empty, four new keyframes. Three pages opened (Kingdom of Manipur, History of Manipur, Anglo-Manipur War); WebFetch returned extracts.

Start year: the court chronicle dates the first king to 33 CE (the History page notes Parratt and Kamei suspect an astrological date) and the infobox start is not recoverable from the extract; the earliest dated acts the pages give are the Loiyamba Shinyen (c. 1110, with the late 11th and early 12th centuries also given), the accession of Khumompa (1263), Kongyapa (1324) and Ningthoukhompa (1432-1467), and the Kingdom page's raid on Akla in 1443. The dossier starts at 1110 at confidence 1; a gap-filler could move the start earlier. The pages date no expansion of the kingdom: the 22,327 km2 figure is 'in the 20th century' and the Kabaw Valley is Manipur's only dated land (1826 to 1834).

Disagreements: Pamheiba's reign 1709-1754 (Kingdom page) or 1709-1748 (History page); the kingdom's present dynasty 1714 (Kingdom page) or 1709; the arrest attempt of 24 March 1891 (Kingdom page) while the Anglo-Manipur War page gives no such date; the British protectorate 'from 1824' (Kingdom page) while the Burmese occupied Manipur until 1826 (History page). The Treaty of Yandabo and Gambhir Singh's reign (1825-1834 on the Kingdom page) are not on the History page. The first treaty with the East India Company (1762, Chingthangkhomba; the kingdom recorded as Meckley) is on the History page and moves no border.

Page silent / not drawn: the Burmese invasions of 1755 and 1758, the conquests of Pamheiba (Tripura, Cachar, the Chindwin), the Kabaw Valley before 1826 and the boundary of the Meitei kingdom before the hill extension; the merger agreement date is on the Kingdom page only (21 September signed, 15 October effective).

Cross-dossier: east-india-company records Manipur's protection as a vassal pair from 1826 (Yandabo page); this dossier dates the protectorate from 1824. Gazetteer: Kabaw Valley is absent (94.35 E 24.2 N, 50 km); Imphal valley is a 45 km disc (93.95 E 24.8 N). The Manipur admin-1 of Natural Earth is used for the 20th-century area.

Suzerainty events kept out of the ledger: vassal_start and vassal_end belong in the suzerain's dossier with this state as the counterpart (the schema: 'counterpart is the vassal itself'), so they are listed here for whoever writes or checks the suzerain. 1824 vassal_start (suzerain east-india-company, confidence 2, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Manipur): 1824: 'From 1824, Manipur became a British protectorate.' Gambhir Singh, 'with British help, expelled the Burmese from Manipur'. The Company page (east-india-company ledger) counts Manipur among the lands Burma ceded at Yandabo in 1826. | 1858-11 vassal_end (suzerain east-india-company, confidence 2, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Manipur_War): 1 November 1858: the Company's rights pass to the Crown (see east-india-company); Manipur continues under the British. The Anglo-Manipur War page notes a Political Agent stationed there since 1835. | 1858-11 vassal_start (suzerain british-raj, confidence 2, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Manipur_War): 1 November 1858: Manipur a protected state under the Crown. | 1947-08 vassal_end (suzerain british-raj, confidence 3, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Manipur): 14 August 1947: 'with the lapse of British paramountcy, Manipur regained the autonomy it had before 1891'; the Manipur State Constitution Act 1947 followed. The Instrument of Accession of 11 August 1947 is disputed.
